Alcohol Consumption Effects on DUI Fatalaties

Budweiser. Guinness. Corona and Bud Light. America’s favorite wheat-based beverage has become nearly synonymous with the American dream. Imagine, for a moment, your next Fourth of July barbecue: fireworks exploding overhead, hot dogs sizzling on the grill, a baseball game on the television in the background. The image would not be complete without a cold one in hand. What so faithfully complements the quintessential American patriot if not an ice cold can of beer?

In order to understand the extent of this obsession, let’s take a look at how the consumption of alcohol has changed among Americans to date.

The above figure depicts the per-capita consumption of alcohol by 21+ individuals in America spanning across the years 1970 to 2022. The amount of alcohol consumption is determined by the ethanol content of each type of beverage, controlling for the varying alcohol percentages. As is clear from the figure, despite its relatively low ethanol-content, beer is still by-and-large the most highly consumed alcoholic beverage by volume in America over the time period. Also, interestingly, there seems to have been a generous decrease in overall alcohol consumption.

Today’s society is replete with advertisements for and the over marketing of alcohol. From online advertisements to television commercials to roadway (the one desired safe haven from the influence of alcohol!) billboards, it seems that there is no way to escape alcohol’s constant presence in our modern world. The alcohol industry spends billions on advertisements every year. For reference, Bud Light and Budweiser were two of the top three Super Bowl advertisers between 2010 and 2020.

Yet, as I hope the opening paragraph of this journal made you feel, this near-romanticism of alcoholic beverages (specifically beer) is a bit excessive, and its ultra-prevalence in American culture makes it even harder to ignore. The negative repercussions that arise from our country’s booze obsession create a moral obligation for us to examine our practices and address their innate faults; this becomes incredibly clear after analyzing the national consumption of alcohol in comparison to DUI fatalities over time. Let’s take a look:

In this figure, we can view the per-capita consumption of beer alongside the DUI fatality rate in each state. By computing the correlation between these two variables, we can find a relatively strong correlation (~0.5) between the number of fatalities in accidents involving alcohol-impaired drivers and gallons of ethanol in beer consumed. It seems that over time and across states, higher beer consumption consistently corresponds with more DUI fatalities.

This correlation does not seem surprising until we take into account the other types of alcohol we have examined thus far. Rather than observing positive relationships, the correlations between DUI fatalities and consumption of other alcohol categories are minimal and even negative!

##   Beverage Type Correlation
## 1       Spirits -0.20787925
## 2          Wine -0.48572878
## 3          Beer  0.49702323
## 4         Total -0.06940748

Now, I would never argue that drinking more of these other spirits would lead to fewer DUI fatalities. Instead, I would like to suggest that due to the informality surrounding beer that has been reinforced by the alcohol industry, people are much more likely to minimize the gravity of driving under its influence. After all, it was just a few beers, right?

Absolutely not. Accidents involving minimally drunk drivers (i.e. drivers with a BAC between 0.01 and 0.07) displayed a similarly strong correlation as to those with more potent BACs. It is important to remain cognizant of our own faculties, as well as those of our friends. Never, ever get behind the wheel while intoxicated, and never, ever let your friends drive drunk. Even if it was “just a few beers.”
